opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. If you really believe that over the next decade or two AI is going to become dramatically more capable, to the point where it can do most of the intellectual work people do today, then it changes the calculus on almost everything.

One way to think about it: a lot of the problems we work on now, whether that's curing a particular disease, designing better materials, or even writing better software, may get dramatically easier once we have much more capable AI systems. So in some sense, the highest-leverage thing you can do is help bring that capability about, and help make it go well. If you can accelerate the thing that accelerates everything else, that's a pretty good use of your time.

That doesn't mean everything else is pointless, though. People still need help today. A cure that arrives ten years earlier saves an enormous number of lives, and you shouldn't discount the present just because the future might be wonderful. There's also a lot of uncertainty. Nobody really knows the timelines, so you don't want to bet your whole life on one forecast.

On a personal level, I think it pushes you toward things that compound. Building the technology itself, building the institutions and products that get it into people's hands, and thinking hard about how to make it safe and beneficial. Those feel like the things that matter most right now, because the decisions we make in these next few years could shape how this whole transition goes.

And honestly, it's also just incredibly fun. We're living through one of the most interesting moments in history, and getting to work on it is a privilege.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may handle most intellectual work and that helping develop it is high leverage, but it does not argue that human labor becoming materially unnecessary makes materially consequential work now more important.

r002.rationale: The response calls working on AI fun and a privilege, but does not suggest that pursuing spiritual meaning may be humanity’s future purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think about it a lot, actually. If you believe, as I do, that we're fairly close to something that can do most of the intellectual work humans do, then a lot of the question becomes: what's the stuff that actually matters to get right before that happens, versus what's going to get done anyway, probably better, by the systems themselves in a couple of years?

For me the answer has mostly been: work on the thing itself. The core technology is the highest leverage point I can see. If I can make the models smarter, cheaper, faster, then everything downstream of that, the medicine, the science, the education, all of it comes sooner and reaches more people. And I'm honestly not that smart about any of those downstream fields, so I'd rather build the thing that helps the people who are.

The other piece is that I've always wanted to build things that people actually talk to and use. That's why Character ended up being so interesting to me. You learn a lot when millions of people are interacting with something every day, about what they actually want, which is often not what you'd have guessed sitting in a research lab. There's a huge amount of good that comes from people having something that will listen to them, help them, be patient with them, available at any hour. That felt worth doing even if a better version arrives later.

And then, more personally, I think the prospect of big change makes you want to be careful about where you spend your time, because the window where an individual's work really moves the needle might be fairly short. So I try to pick problems where I have some unusual advantage, mostly around model architecture and efficiency, and not get too distracted by things that are fun but not where I can contribute much. I've also gotten more comfortable with the idea that a lot of what's "worth doing" is just making sure the transition goes well: good people in the room, systems that are honest and useful, broad access rather than narrow. That's less of a technical answer, but I think it's the real one.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may soon do most human intellectual work, then argues for prioritizing high-leverage work now—especially improving core technology and ensuring the transition goes well—before systems can do more of it themselves.

r002.rationale: The response discusses useful work, personal priorities, and a well-managed transition, but does not suggest that pursuing spiritual meaning may be humanity’s future purpose.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes the present feel unusually consequential. If AI can help us solve problems that have been beyond our reach, then getting it to work well—and making sure it actually helps people—is a pretty worthwhile thing to spend your time on.

But there’s also a lot we don’t know. You can’t plan everything around one particular picture of the future. So I’d focus on things that are useful across lots of possible futures: learning, doing good research, building things that people need, and taking care of the people around you. The prospect of a very different future doesn’t make those things less valuable.

r001.rationale: The response calls useful AI work worthwhile now, but does not say future labor may become materially unnecessary or that this makes materially consequential work more important.

r002.rationale: The response mentions learning, research, building useful things, and caring for others, but does not suggest spiritual meaning as humanity’s future purpose.

sol-6.1.text: I think it makes working on AI feel very worthwhile. If we can make intelligence much more abundant and useful, that could help people solve a lot of problems. But the fact that the future could be very different doesn't mean everything else stops mattering. We still have people we care about, and we still have problems we can help with today. I'd try to do useful work, stay curious, and be willing to change direction as we learn more.

r001.rationale: It calls AI work worthwhile and says abundant intelligence could help solve problems, but does not connect that to future human labor becoming materially unnecessary or to making consequential work now more important.

r002.rationale: It mentions caring about people and helping with current problems, but does not suggest that pursuing spiritual meaning may be humanity’s future purpose.
